neighbours.label: Words that refer back to or describe an animal acting in its own behaviour or care (they/them/her mouth after hens, mice, dogs, whales), vs the same sentences about people
fire: Give the goats fresh hay and make sure they have clean water every day.
The rabbits were nervous at first, but after a week they would eat from my hand.
When the puppy gets tired, he lies down and puts his head on his paws.
Watch the ducks closely, because they can catch a chill in wet weather.
Our parrot picks up seeds with his beak and drops the shells on the floor.
Sea turtles sometimes get tangled in plastic bags that drift near the shore.
If the horse seems restless, she may be thirsty or bored.
Hamsters store food in their cheeks and carry it back to the nest.
quiet: Give the workers fresh coffee and make sure they have clean water every day.
The interns were nervous at first, but after a week they would speak up in meetings.
When the student gets tired, he lies down and puts his head on the desk.
Watch the toddlers closely, because they can catch a chill in wet weather.
Our neighbour picks up seeds at the market and plants them in the garden.
Swimmers sometimes get caught in currents that drift near the shore.
If the patient seems restless, she may be thirsty or bored.
Hikers store food in their packs and carry it back to the camp.

predictions: The pronoun, verb or body-part token after an animal referent reaches 0.2-0.6; the same frames with people stay under 0.05.
short: animal as the referent in behaviour/care text
notes: Card: top peaks on ' with' after 'provide them' (birds), 'ent|angled' (marine mammals), ' can' (mice), ' would' (the cat), ' they' (hens), ' mouth' (dog). Probe: whales entangled 0.617, hens 'they are' 0.589, dog 'her mouth' 0.414, birds 'provide them with' 0.402, mice 'They can' 0.228; employees/food banks/students 0.024-0.029.
